The initial energy content of the egg in Marbled crayfish (Procambarus virginalis) has been estimated by drawing upon published data for related species. Based on an egg diameter of 1.5 millimeters in this parthenogenetic decapod, and applying a scaling relationship from the energetics of Cherax quadricarinatus eggs, the yolk of a single P. virginalis zygote contains approximately 37.6 joules . This modest initial energetic investment is consistent with the small size of the newly hatched individuals, which measure only 0.35 centimeters  in total length at the moment of eclosion, a period when the lecithotrophic larva relies entirely on its remaining yolk reserves. The chorionate embryo undergoes a predictable developmental sequence under controlled laboratory conditions. When incubated at a stable water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the first feeding stage, marked by the trophic switch to exogenous food sources, occurs after approximately 20 days , at which point the young juvenile has already absorbed the majority of its yolk.

Upon successful eclosion and subsequent yolk-sac resorption, the growing juveniles begin a phase of rapid mass increase. At the point of birth, which follows a brood care period of approximately 25 days spent attached to the pleopods of the ovigerous female, these recently independent individuals have a wet weight of only 0.0053 grams [Wwb = 0.0053 grams]. Their total length at this stage is 0.57 centimeters [Lb = 0.57 centimeters], a modest size that belies the accelerated growth trajectory to come. The complete transition from the hatching event to the free-living juvenile stage, encompassing both embryonic development and the subsequent period of maternal attendance, takes approximately 45 days [ab = approximately 45 days] when the animals are maintained at a constant 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This interval includes the non-feeding, endotrophic phase immediately post-hatching, during which the young crayfish continue to rely on internal yolk stores before commencing active foraging on microbial biofilms and detritus.

Reproductive maturity in Procambarus virginalis is attained after a defined period of somatic growth in a stable thermal environment. Under a rearing temperature regime of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the time since birth at puberty is approximately 220 days [tp = approximately 220 days]. The total length at puberty for this species is 4 centimeters [Lp = 4 centimeters], marking a key milestone in the transition from a pre-reproductive juvenile to a breeding individual. The wet weight at puberty, measured in individuals that have just become reproductively active, is 1.537 grams [Wwp = 1.537 grams], a value that reflects the considerable mass gain achieved during the juvenile growth phase. The onset of gonadal activity in this triploid species is rapid compared to many other crayfish, which is a direct consequence of its parthenogenetic reproductive mode, as every individual is capable of producing offspring. Following the attainment of puberty, females proceed to produce their first clutch of eggs as part of their ongoing reproductive cycle.

Once females attain sexual maturation, their reproductive output is considerable under optimal conditions. The maximum reproductive rate, expressed as the combination of clutch size and spawning frequency, has been reported for this species when it is held at 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Detailed laboratory observations indicate that berried females produce an average of 450 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 450 eggs per clutch], and they are capable of producing a new clutch approximately every 8 weeks [F_R_i = clutch approximately every 8 weeks], a high frequency enabled by their uniparental reproductive strategy. This prodigious fecundity allows a single individual to quickly populate a novel habitat, which partly explains the invasive success of the marbled crayfish across European freshwater ecosystems. The rapid turnover of broods and the substantial number of offspring per spawning event distinguish P. virginalis from many gonochoristic decapod species with slower life-history strategies.

In terms of ultimate size and longevity, lab-reared individuals of Procambarus virginalis can attain considerable dimensions. The ultimate total length, measured from the tip of the rostrum to the end of the telson, reaches 10 centimeters [Li = 10 centimeters] in the largest specimens, while the ultimate carapace length alone is 4.5 centimeters . The maximum recorded wet weight for captive individuals is 30 grams [Wwi = 30 grams], though a slightly larger specimen of 32 grams has been documented in nature, suggesting that wild populations may occasionally exceed the growth limits observed in the laboratory. Regarding lifespan, the most long-lived decile of the population, as documented in a long-term laboratory study at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], exhibited a mean longevity of 1154 days [am = 1154 days]. This comparatively extended adult phase allows for numerous successive spawning events over an individual's lifetime, contributing to its high invasive potential.
